title: Κύων ⟨λέοντα διώκων⟩ καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Dog Chasing a Lion and the Fox
part: The Dog Chasing a Lion and the Fox (Chambry 187)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 187. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κύων θηρευτικὸς λέοντα ἰδών, τοῦτον ἐδίωκεν.
sentences.tr: Kyōn thēreutikos leonta idōn, touton ediōken.
sentences.l: A hunting dog, having seen a lion, was pursuing him.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ ἐπιστραφεὶς ὁ λέων ἐβρυχήσατο, φοβηθεὶς εἰς τοὐπίσω ἔφυγεν.
sentences.tr: Hōs de epistrapheis ho leōn ebrychēsato, phobētheis eis toupisō ephygen.
sentences.l: But when the lion, having turned about, roared, he, having taken fright, fled backwards.
sentences.i: But when the lion turned and roared, the dog took fright and fled back.
sentences.n: τοὐπίσω is crasis, τὸ ὀπίσω run together into one word: the rear, what lies behind. ὡς with the aorist indicative is temporal here, "when", not "as" or "since".

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ θεασαμένη αὐτὸν ἔφη· « Ὦ κακὴ κεφαλή, σὺ λέοντα ἐδίωκες, οὗ οὐδὲ τὸν βρυχηθμὸν ὑπέμεινας ; »
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de theasamenē auton ephē· « Ō kakē kephalē, sy leonta ediōkes, hou oude ton brychēthmon hypemeinas ; »
sentences.l: And a fox, having beheld him, said: « O wicked head, you were chasing a lion, whose roar you did not even withstand? »
sentences.i: And a fox, seeing him, said: « You wretched creature, you were chasing a lion whose roar you could not even endure? »
sentences.n: ὦ κακὴ κεφαλή is abuse and not description: κεφαλή stands for the whole man in address, as English says "you fool" rather than naming a part. The imperfect ἐδίωκες throws his own performance back at him — this is what you were doing. οὗ is a relative genitive hanging on τὸν βρυχηθμόν: the roar of the lion he was chasing.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος λεχθείη ἂν ἐπ’ ἀνδρῶν αὐθάδων οἳ κατὰ πολὺ δυνατωτέρων συκοφαντεῖν ἐπιχειροῦντες, ὅταν ἐκεῖνοι ἀντιστῶσιν, εὐθέως ἀναχαιτίζουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos lechtheiē an ep’ andrōn authadōn hoi kata poly dynatōterōn sykophantein epicheirountes, hotan ekeinoi antistōsin, eutheōs anachaitizousin.
sentences.l: The story might be told of self-willed men who, setting their hands to bringing malicious charges against men far more powerful, whenever those men stand against them, at once rear back.
sentences.i: The story might be told of presumptuous men who set about slandering those far stronger than themselves, and the moment the others stand up to them, back off at once.
sentences.n: λεχθείη ἄν is the potential optative, the collection's mild "might be told". ἀναχαιτίζω belongs to horses — to throw the head and mane back, to shy and refuse — and the picture is exactly the dog's about-turn. συκοφαντέω is not idle slander but the professional bringing of a vexatious charge. κατά here governs the genitive δυνατωτέρων, "against men more powerful", with πολύ strengthening the comparative; the words look like the fixed adverbial κατὰ πολύ, "by far", but that reading would leave the genitive with nothing to govern it.
